name: Bromelain

lead: Bromelain is a mixture of protein-digesting enzymes extracted mainly from pineapple stem. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing; a topical form is approved for debriding burn wounds.
In appearance contexts it is used to reduce post-procedure swelling and bruising (for example after cosmetic surgery) and general inflammation. Study results are mixed and often small.

paras: Bromelain's proteolytic activity is thought to modulate inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins and to affect fibrin breakdown. How much active enzyme survives digestion and reaches tissue after oral dosing is uncertain.

Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to pineapple. It may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and interact with some antibiotics. Supplement potency is inconsistent. Legal as a supplement.

lead: Bromelain is an extract from pineapple, mainly the stem, containing a mixture of protein-digesting enzymes and smaller amounts of other compounds [1]. The best-known enzymes are stem bromelain and fruit bromelain, both sulfhydryl (cysteine) proteases [1]. It is used industrially as a meat tenderiser and in baking and cosmetics manufacturing, and is sold as an oral supplement, often aimed at swelling, bruising and general inflammation [1][2].

According to Wikipedia, the only approved clinical use is a topical enzyme preparation, NexoBrid, authorised in Europe in 2012 for removing dead tissue from severe burns; for other uses, bromelain supplements are marketed without confirmed efficacy, dosage or interaction data [1]. Systematic reviews of clinical studies cover surgery-related oedema and pain, osteoarthritis, and other inflammation-related conditions, with heterogeneous and often small trials [3][4][5].

In looksmaxxing and physique communities bromelain is discussed chiefly as a way to reduce swelling and bruising after cosmetic procedures, as a recovery aid for training, and as a digestive enzyme [6][7][8].
infobox: Sold as a dietary supplement in many countries

paras: Commercial bromelain is an extract rather than a single molecule. It is a mixture of sulfhydryl proteases plus minor components, and the term has been applied both to the individual enzymes and to the whole extract [1]. It is produced mostly in pineapple-growing countries such as Thailand and Malaysia from stems, peel, leaves or processing waste, which are blended, filtered, purified and concentrated [1].

The enzymes are heat labile: cooked or canned pineapple does not tenderise meat, and the amount in an ordinary serving of fruit is probably small compared with extracted supplements [1]. Because composition and enzyme activity vary between products, reviews note that potency is not uniform across supplements [2].

Pineapple has a long tradition of medicinal use among peoples of South and Central America [1][4]. Bromelain was first isolated in 1891 by the Venezuelan chemist Vicente Marcano through fermenting pineapple fruit. In 1892 Russell Chittenden and colleagues studied it more fully and named it bromelin; the term bromelain was later introduced and originally used for proteases from any plant of the family Bromeliaceae [1].

A 1969 controlled clinical report in a plastic-surgery journal described bromelain as a proteolytic enzyme in the context of tissue swelling, an early link between the extract and surgical recovery [9]. A 2006 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery later summarised its use in that field [10].

Bromelain is promoted for reducing swelling and bruising after facial and body procedures, and sometimes combined with arnica. A registered trial is evaluating it for facial swelling after jaw surgery, and a trial of arnica with bromelain after rhinoplasty was registered but withdrawn [11][12]. An over-the-counter bruising supplement listed on DailyMed combines bromelain with arnica, vitamin C, zinc and bioflavonoids, describing itself as nutritional support during recovery [13].

The established medical product is topical: a bromelain-enriched enzyme concentrate for debridement of severe burn wounds [1]. Oral bromelain has been studied for osteoarthritis, sinusitis, post-operative swelling in dental and plastic surgery, ulcerative colitis, and as an adjunct in oncology and infection research [3][14][15][16].

Reviews describe antioedematous, anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic and fibrinolytic activities of bromelain in vitro and in animals, and propose that these depend in part on proteolytic activity, with the active factors only partly characterised [2]. A 2025 systematic review of in vitro studies found that bromelain reduced secretion of the cytokines IL-1 beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha from stimulated immune cells [5]. Proposed effects on bradykinin, prostaglandins and fibrin breakdown appear in reviews of its pharmacology [2][14].

A 2023 systematic review reported that bromelain can be detected in serum with retained proteolytic activity after oral intake, but how much reaches tissues and whether this explains clinical effects remains discussed in the literature [3][2].

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis covering 54 articles, 39 of which were meta-analysed, assessed efficacy and safety of bromelain across conditions and reported heterogeneity among studies [3]. A 2024 systematic review in Nutrients and a 2021 review summarised possible applications in cardiovascular, inflammatory, infectious and oncological contexts while stating that further mechanistic and clinical work is needed [4][14].

Surgical settings have received the most attention. A double-blind randomised trial of 114 breast-conserving surgery patients tested a supplement containing bromelain with Boswellia phytosome, with or without alpha-lipoic acid, superoxide dismutase, vitamins and centella, versus placebo for 30 days; the combination arm showed less oedema than placebo, so the effect cannot be attributed to bromelain alone [17]. Other trials examined oral bromelain after periodontal surgery and third-molar extraction [15][18], and an ulcerative colitis trial and a dental plaque enzyme pre-rinse trial have been published [16][19].

Registered trials include studies on facial swelling after jaw surgery, third-molar surgery, diabetic foot ulcers, root-canal medication, cough, and intratumoral use in pseudomyxoma peritonei [11][20][21][22][23][24]. No large randomised trial of oral bromelain for cosmetic-procedure bruising in healthy people appears among the published studies reviewed.

Reviews describe bromelain as having low toxicity and few side effects [2][14]. A DailyMed label for a bromelain-containing bruising supplement lists mild gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea and skin rash, rare hypersensitivity reactions and prolonged bleeding as possible reactions, and advises caution with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs and stopping use two weeks before surgery [13].

Allergic reactions are listed on the same label [13]. One T Nation user on dual antiplatelet therapy after stent placement reported spontaneous gum bleeding when adding bromelain, which he took as a warning sign [25].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and training communities
paras: On T Nation, bromelain appears in individual supplement lists alongside fish oil, collagen, glucosamine and CoQ10 [6][26], in discussions of tendon and elbow pain management [8], and as a digestive-enzyme suggestion during bulking [7]. A poster recalled that retail supplement shops sold it for anti-inflammatory purposes and asked whether pineapple juice was used for the same reason [27]. Another forum user suggested a daily bromelain and NAC regimen in a COVID-19 thread [28]. Discussion is largely anecdotal.
Bromelain is sold as a dietary supplement; the only regulatory approval cited by Wikipedia is the European authorisation of the topical burn debridement product [1].

lore.intro: In training and recovery forums bromelain is described as a pineapple-derived anti-inflammatory and enzyme supplement, mentioned in stacks for joints, bruising and digestion [8][6][7].

claims.claim: Bromelain reduces swelling and bruising after injury or surgery
Eating pineapple provides the same benefits as the supplement
It acts as a digestive enzyme that helps with large food intake
Bromelain can thin the blood and cause bleeding with antiplatelet drugs
